title: They liked you more than you think.
body: After a conversation, people consistently underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed it. Psychologists call it the liking gap. Your small message probably landed better than you fear.
cite: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark, Psychological Science, 2018

title: Friendship is built in hours.
body: One study found it takes about 50 hours together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, and more than 200 to become close friends. Every coffee, walk and call is a real deposit.
cite: Hall, Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 2018

title: Voices connect.
body: People expect a call to feel awkward, but hearing someone's voice creates a stronger bond than text, and it's rarely as awkward as they feared.
cite: Kumar & Epley, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2021

title: Appreciation lands harder than you think.
body: People who express gratitude underestimate how happy it will make the other person, and overestimate how awkward it will feel.
cite: Kumar & Epley, Psychological Science, 2018

title: Awe makes worries smaller.
body: Moments of awe, like vast views, night skies or big music, shrink the sense of self, ease rumination and make people more generous.
cite: Keltner & Haidt, 2003; Piff et al., 2015

title: Picture your best possible self.
body: Writing for a few minutes about a future where things went well lifts mood and optimism, and makes your goals feel more real.
cite: King, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2001

title: Plans beat willpower.
body: Deciding exactly when and where you'll do something (“At 7 pm at my desk, I will…”) makes you far more likely to follow through.
cite: Gollwitzer, American Psychologist, 1999

title: Talk to yourself like a friend.
body: Treating yourself with the kindness you'd offer a friend is linked to less anxiety and more resilience. It doesn't make you lazy; it makes you more likely to try again.
cite: Neff, 2003; Breines & Chen, 2012

title: Celebrate their good news.
body: How you respond when someone shares good news matters a lot. Enthusiastic, curious replies (“That's huge, tell me everything!”) are linked to closer, more satisfying relationships.
cite: Gable, Reis, Impett & Asher, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2004

title: Go deeper than small talk.
body: People expect deep conversations to feel awkward and less enjoyable than shallow ones. In practice, they feel more connected and enjoy them more than they predicted. The other person usually wants to go deeper too.
cite: Kardas, Kumar & Epley, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2022

title: Strangers are friendlier than you think.
body: Commuters asked to talk to a stranger expected a worse ride. They actually had a more pleasant one, and nobody got rebuffed. We underestimate how much others want to chat.
cite: Epley & Schroeder, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2014

title: Small hellos count.
body: On days when people chatted with more acquaintances, like a barista, a classmate or a neighbor, they felt happier and more like they belonged. Light ties matter, not just close ones.
cite: Sandstrom & Dunn, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2014

title: People want to say yes.
body: When people ask strangers for small favors, they underestimate how many will agree, often by about half. Asking feels bigger to you than it does to them.
cite: Flynn & Lake, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2008

title: Say the nice thing.
body: People who give compliments underestimate how good they make the other person feel, and overestimate how awkward it will be. The warm thought in your head is worth saying out loud.
cite: Boothby & Bohns, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2021

title: Kindness comes back to you.
body: Across dozens of studies, doing kind things for others gave a real, if modest, lift to the well-being of the person being kind. Small acts count.
cite: Curry et al., Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2018

title: Proximity makes friends.
body: In a classic study of student housing, people were most likely to become friends with whoever lived closest. Seeing the same faces again and again is how strangers turn into friends.
cite: Festinger, Schachter & Back, Social Pressures in Informal Groups, 1950

title: New places, brighter days.
body: Tracking people's movements for months, researchers found that on days with more variety in where people went, they felt happier. Novelty and good mood travel together.
cite: Heller et al., Nature Neuroscience, 2020

title: Two hours a week outside.
body: In a study of about 20,000 people, those who spent at least 120 minutes a week in nature were more likely to report good health and high well-being. It didn't matter how they split it up.
cite: White et al., Scientific Reports, 2019

title: Green walks quiet the loop.
body: People who took a 90-minute walk in nature replayed negative thoughts less afterward than people who walked along a busy road. The setting of a walk matters.
cite: Bratman, Hamilton, Hahn, Daily & Gross, PNAS, 2015

title: Moving together bonds people.
body: Dancing or singing in time with others raises feelings of closeness. Groups who sang together bonded faster than groups doing crafts or writing.
cite: Tarr, Launay, Cohen & Dunbar, Biology Letters, 2015; Pearce, Launay & Dunbar, Royal Society Open Science, 2015

title: Stay with the good part.
body: Savoring means noticing a good moment and letting it last a little longer. On days people savored their good experiences, those experiences lifted their mood more.
cite: Jose, Lim & Bryant, Journal of Positive Psychology, 2012

title: Movement lifts mood.
body: In data from over a million Americans, people who exercised reported about 1.5 fewer bad mental-health days a month. Team sports, cycling and gym workouts showed the strongest links, and any movement helped.
cite: Chekroud et al., The Lancet Psychiatry, 2018

title: Write it out.
body: People who wrote about upsetting experiences for about 15 minutes, four days in a row, had better health and mood in the months after. Getting it on paper helps make sense of it.
cite: Pennebaker & Beall, Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 1986

title: Small wins add up.
body: In about 12,000 work diary entries, the biggest boost to people's mood and motivation was simply making progress on something meaningful, even a small step.
cite: Amabile & Kramer, The Progress Principle, 2011

title: Find your flow.
body: Flow is that state where time disappears because you're absorbed. It shows up when a task is a stretch, but not too much of one, for your skills. Those moments are clues to what fits you.
cite: Csikszentmihalyi, Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience, 1990

title: Notice what went right.
body: Writing down three things that went well each day, and why, for one week, left people happier for up to six months.
cite: Seligman, Steen, Park & Peterson, American Psychologist, 2005

title: Switch off to recharge.
body: Recovery from a demanding week comes from four things: mentally detaching, relaxing, learning something new and choosing how you spend your time. Rest is a skill.
cite: Sonnentag & Fritz, Journal of Occupational Health Psychology, 2007

title: Remember what matters to you.
body: Writing for a few minutes about a value that matters to you, and why, helps people stay steadier under stress and pressure. It reminds you that you're bigger than one hard moment.
cite: Cohen & Sherman, Annual Review of Psychology, 2014

title: Making art calms the body.
body: After 45 minutes of making art, most participants had lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol, whatever their skill or experience. Talent not required.
cite: Kaimal, Ray & Muniz, Art Therapy, 2016

title: Helping helps the helper.
body: Volunteers report more happiness, life satisfaction and sense of control. The link runs both ways: giving time lifts well-being, and feeling good makes people give more.
cite: Thoits & Hewitt, Journal of Health and Social Behavior, 2001
